summary: Specifies how multiple multicast VPNs or EVPN broadcast domains can share a single point-to-multipoint tunnel using common labels, instead of each needing its own upstream-assigned MPLS label. It updates RFC 6514, RFC 7432, and RFC 7582.

eli5.summary: Several families can share one bus if everyone agrees on the same seat labels. This lets many virtual networks share one delivery tunnel with common labels.

questions: what is the domain wide common block
what is an upstream assigned mpls label
how do mvpn and evpn share a p2mp tunnel
subtitle: How many VPNs and broadcast domains can share one multicast tunnel without every router tracking a million labels.

tldr.problem: When one multicast tunnel carries traffic for many VPNs or broadcast domains, each ingress router picks its own upstream-assigned MPLS labels. Every egress router must then track a separate label space for every ingress router, which can add up to around a million labels.
tldr.mechanism: Labels for each VPN, broadcast domain or Ethernet segment are provisioned centrally so that all routers use the same one. They come either from a Domain-wide Common Block (DCB) of the normal label space or from a few shared context-specific label spaces, and BGP routes signal which case applies.
tldr.outcome: The number of labels needed falls to roughly the number of VPNs, domains and segments. The RFC adds a DCB flag and a new extended community, and updates RFC 6514, RFC 7432 and RFC 7582.

facts.label: DCB flag
facts.value: Bit 47 in Additional PMSI Tunnel Attribute Flags

today: RFC 9573 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2024 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 6514, RFC 7432 and RFC 7582.

sections.title: Aggregate Tunnels and Upstream Labels
sections.content:
A Multicast VPN (MVPN) can carry customer multicast traffic across a provider backbone using Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) tunnels. Often a tunnel serves one VPN, but the specifications also allow an aggregate tunnel that carries several VPNs. EVPN does the same for its Broadcast Domains (BDs). BIER transport behaves much like an aggregate tunnel from the MVPN or EVPN point of view, and the RFC uses the term aggregate tunnels for both.

On an aggregate tunnel, the ingress Provider Edge (PE) router allocates an upstream-assigned MPLS label for each VPN or BD. Each packet carries the label the ingress PE bound to the packet's VPN or BD.

The egress PE has to interpret that label in the context of the ingress PE. So for each ingress PE it keeps a context-specific label space and looks the label up there.
sections.eli5: Each sender writes its own numbers on the packages. The receiver needs a separate decoder sheet for every sender to know what a number means.

sections.title: The Scaling Problem
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example: 1001 PEs, each hosting 1000 VPNs or BDs. Each ingress PE assigns 1000 labels, and because the PEs do not coordinate, each egress PE must be ready to interpret 1,000,000 upstream-assigned labels across 1000 context-specific label spaces.

The same problem exists for EVPN ESI labels used for multihoming. With 1001 PEs each attached to 1000 Ethernet Segments, each PE may need to understand 1,000,000 ESI labels, even when no tunnel aggregation is used.

The RFC notes that few if any deployments used aggregate tunnels so far, but expects more use. A single EVPN tenant may have many BDs, and BIER is becoming more attractive as MVPN/EVPN transport.
sections.eli5: With a thousand senders each using a thousand numbers, the receiver ends up with a mountain of decoder sheets.

sections.title: Common Labels and the DCB
sections.content:
The idea is that a central entity assigns one label to each VPN, BD or ES, and every PE uses that same label. The number of labels then equals the sum of the VPNs, BDs and ESs. The RFC reaches this by reserving part of the default label space as the Domain-wide Common Block (DCB), similar to using identical SRGBs on all nodes. For example, all PEs could reserve a DCB of [1000~2000] and be provisioned so that label 1000 maps to VPN 0, label 1001 to VPN 1, and so on.

If a DCB big enough for everything is impractical, labels can come from one or a few context-specific label spaces that are not tied to any one PE. Each such space is identified by a label from the DCB. The ingress PE imposes the service labels first and then the DCB label that names the label space.

The 'domain' only needs to include the PEs of an MVPN/EVPN. Internal P routers are better left out, since these labels only reach the top of the label stack at the PEs.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees on one shared list of seat numbers in advance. If the list is too long, a short code at the front says which list to use.

sections.title: MP2MP Tunnels and Segmented Tunnels
sections.content:
For Multipoint-to-Multipoint (MP2MP) tunnels used with an MVPN, RFC 7582 has the tunnel root allocate PE Distinguisher Labels. This RFC requires that the PE Distinguisher Labels a node allocates come from the same label space that node uses for its VPN-identifying labels.

Tunnel segmentation adds a wrinkle. For selective tunnels (S-PMSIs), a segmentation point may need to switch two flows from one tunnel in one region onto two different tunnels in the next region. That requires different labels for the two S-PMSI routes, so a central entity cannot hand out domain-wide labels for them. Instead, each PE is assigned its own disjoint label block within the few context-specific label spaces (for example [101~200] for PE1 and [201~300] for PE2) and allocates from it. Per-PE and per-AS/region tunnels need a label per PMSI route, and the RFC prefers per-region PMSIs because per-PE ones keep the original scaling issue.

As an alternative, segmentation points can do (C-S,C-G) lookups in VRFs, which moves the scaling problem from label count to route count.
sections.eli5: When packages must be re-sorted halfway along, each depot gets its own private range of numbers so they never clash.

sections.title: Signaling and Procedures
sections.content:
The RFC defines three allocation methods. In Option 1 a central entity allocates per-VPN/BD/ES labels from the DCB. In Option 2 it allocates them from a few common context-specific label spaces and uses DCB labels to identify those spaces. In Option 3 it also gives each PE a disjoint block in those spaces for segmented S-PMSIs. Option 1 is simplest but needs a DCB large enough for everything. These procedures MAY be used, but if they are, all PEs and segmentation points MUST support them.

Signaling uses two BGP markers. A DCB-flag (bit 47 in the Additional PMSI Tunnel Attribute Flags) means the label in the route's PTA comes from the DCB. A Context-Specific Label Space ID Extended Community means the label comes from an identified context-specific space.

  • A route MUST carry the DCB-flag if and only if its PTA label is from the DCB.
  • A route MUST NOT carry both. A received route with both is treated as withdrawn.
  • With neither, the label is the old upstream-assigned label from the source PE's space.
  • A receiver MUST install a forwarding entry mapping the label in the extended community to the context-specific label table.

If a PE originates two routes with the same tunnel, they must all agree on using or not using each marker, otherwise receivers treat the routes as withdrawn. The ES label and BD label MUST come from the same label space.
sections.eli5: A little sticker on each announcement says which list the number comes from. Announcements with confusing or contradictory stickers are thrown out.

sections.title: The Context-Specific Label Space ID Extended Community
sections.content:
The new extended community is a Transitive Opaque extended community whose first octet is 0x03 or 0x43, followed by sub-type 0x08 (assigned by IANA). It carries a 2-octet ID-Type and a 4-octet ID-Value.

This RFC defines only ID-Type 0, which means the ID-Value is a label. The most significant 20 bits of the ID-Value hold the label value. IANA created a registry for the ID types, with 0 as MPLS Label, 1 to 254 unassigned and 255 reserved, under First Come First Served.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny tag that says 'look in list number such-and-such'.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC argues that Option 1 is equivalent to common SRGBs from the regular per-platform label space, Option 2 to common SRGBs from a third-party label space, and Option 3 to a variation with disjoint blocks. In all cases a receiving PE can identify one of a few label forwarding tables.

RFC 6514, RFC 7432, RFC 8402 and RFC 5331 list no security concerns about label allocation, and this document introduces no new ones.

IANA registered bit 47 (DCB) in the Additional PMSI Tunnel Attribute Flags registry, sub-type 0x08 for the new extended community, and created the Context-Specific Label Space ID Type registry.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about, because the receiver still just looks numbers up in a few known lists.
